title: Monetary Policy Report – July 2018
summary: The Federal Reserve's July 2018 Monetary Policy Report documents labor market strengthening during H1 2018, with nonfarm payrolls averaging 215,000/month and the unemployment rate declining to 4.0% in June—below all FOMC participants' longer-run estimates. The report includes a detailed analysis of prime-age labor force participation trends, examining factors including education levels, disability, caregiving, and automation impacts on workforce participation.
key_points: Nonfarm payrolls averaged 215,000 jobs/month in H1 2018, above 2017 pace and well above labor force entry requirements
Unemployment rate fell to 4.0% in June 2018, below all FOMC participants' longer-run estimates and approximately 0.5pp below the median
Prime-age (25-54) labor force participation rates rose consistently since 2013 as improving labor market conditions drew workers back
Long-run decline in prime-age LFPR attributed partly to secular decline in demand for workers without college degrees, linked to automation and globalization
Baby-boom cohort aging drives overall LFPR downward trend; 65+ share of population projected to rise from 16% (2000) to 24% (2026)
Involuntary part-time work fell close to pre-recession levels, indicating tightening labor market conditions
why_it_matters: This report provides the Fed's official assessment of labor market conditions as of mid-2018, during a period of tightening labor markets and ongoing rate normalization. The analysis of labor force participation trends—including structural factors like automation, education shifts, and caregiving—remains relevant for understanding longer-run labor supply constraints. The report was submitted to Congress on July 13, 2018, ahead of FOMC decisions during that period.
macro_context: Historical labor market analysis from July 2018. The data describes conditions significantly different from current (2026) labor market dynamics. At the time, unemployment at 4.0% was considered below longer-run normal levels. Job growth was strong at 215k/month average, and labor force participation was trending upward for prime-age workers. The report discusses structural factors limiting labor supply growth, including automation reducing demand for non-college-educated workers and demographic aging.
